b: A short letter to a small church Paul had never visited, which was being drawn towards a ‘philosophy’ that added rules, rituals and spiritual experiences to Christ. Paul’s answer is to make the largest possible claims about him: he is ‘the image of the invisible God’, the one through whom and for whom all things were made, in whom ‘all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form’. Believers have everything in him.

The second half shows what that means for ordinary life: setting the mind on things above, putting off the old self, forgiving, and living out faith at home and at work. Colossians 1:15–20 is the passage most often discussed with Jehovah’s Witnesses, and repays careful reading.

Colossae lay in the Lycus valley in the Roman province of Asia (today south-west Turkey), about 120 miles (190 km) east of Ephesus. Centuries earlier it had been an important city on the main road east, famous for its wool. By Paul’s time the road had been moved and its neighbours had overtaken it: Laodicea, about 11 miles away, and Hierapolis. Colossae had become a small country town.

Paul had never been there (2:1). The church was founded by Epaphras, a Colossian (1:7; 4:12), probably while Paul was teaching in Ephesus and ‘all who lived in the province of Asia’ heard the word (Acts 19:10). Philemon and his slave Onesimus belonged to this church.
Unlike Ephesus or Philippi, Colossae has never been properly excavated. The site is still an unexcavated mound near the modern town of Honaz, with only traces of a small theatre visible.

b: The Roman historian Tacitus records that in AD 60, ‘Laodicea, one of the famous Asiatic cities, was laid in ruins by an earthquake, but recovered by its own resources’, without help from Rome. Colossae, a few miles away, will have suffered too. The letter does not mention any disaster, which suggests it was written before the earthquake, or before news of it reached Paul. This is one reason many date the letter to about AD 60 or a little earlier.

b: Where scholars stand. Since the 19th century some scholars have doubted that Paul wrote Colossians, and many today call it a ‘disputed’ letter. Their reasons: it has many words not found in Paul’s other letters; its long, flowing sentences differ in style; it uses ‘church’ of the worldwide church; it says believers have already been raised with Christ (2:12; 3:1); and its teaching about Christ’s rule over the universe seems more developed. Some suggest a follower of Paul wrote it after his death. Opinion is genuinely divided; many scholars, including some who doubt Ephesians, still accept Colossians as Paul’s.

The case for Paul. (1) The letter names Paul three times and ends with a greeting ‘in my own hand’ (4:18), the mark Paul used to show a letter was really his (2 Thessalonians 3:17). (2) It is tied tightly to Philemon, which almost all scholars accept as Paul’s: the same people send greetings (Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke), Onesimus is being sent home, and Archippus is mentioned in both. As C. F. D. Moule put it, it seems ‘impossible to doubt that Philemon was written by St Paul, or to doubt the close connection between Philemon and Colossians.’ It is hard to imagine a later writer inventing such ordinary, checkable details. (3) Differences of words and style are what we would expect when someone writes about a new problem, perhaps using a secretary (Timothy is co-sender, 1:1). Recent scholars put less weight on the vocabulary argument. (4) The high view of Christ is not new: Philippians 2:6–11, which no one doubts, is just as exalted. (5) Paul never set out his theology as a fixed system; each letter answers a particular situation.

When and where? Paul is in prison (4:3, 10, 18). Rome (about AD 60) is the traditional answer; Ephesus (mid-50s) and Caesarea (late 50s) have also been proposed. Colossians, Philemon and Ephesians were probably written at the same time, since Tychicus carries both Colossians and Ephesians (4:7; Ephesians 6:21).

b: Paul warns against a ‘philosophy and empty deception’ (2:8) but never names it, and scholars have proposed many identities: an early form of Gnosticism, Jewish mysticism, a Jewish group insisting on the law, or a local mixture of Jewish and pagan folk religion. From the letter we can see that it involved food rules and holy days (2:16), harsh treatment of the body (2:21–23), visions, and ‘the worship of angels’ (2:18). Clinton Arnold points to evidence that people in Phrygia called on angels for protection against evil powers. Whatever it was exactly, it did not deny Christ outright; it treated him as not enough. Paul’s whole answer is that Christ is everything.

1.t: Image of the invisible God, firstborn over all creation, the one in whom all things were created and hold together, the head of the body, the one in whom all fullness dwells. Firstborn here is rank, not birth order — Psalm 89:27 calls David firstborn though he was the youngest son.
Paul says all things were created in him, through him and for him. Greek had words for 'other' and he used neither, which is why insertions at this verse change the argument rather than clarify it.

1.h: Christ in you, the hope of glory
1.t: The mystery hidden for ages and now disclosed. Paul's labour is described as struggling with energy that God supplies.

2.t: The Colossian error added ritual, mystical experience and ascetic rules to Christ. Paul's answer is that all the fullness of deity dwells in him bodily, and that believers have been filled in him — nothing is missing that needs supplementing.
The record of charges against us was nailed to the cross. The image is of a handwritten IOU cancelled.

3.t: The basis of Christian ethics in this letter is not effort but identity: you died, your life is hidden with Christ, therefore live accordingly.

The virtue list is corporate — compassion, kindness, humility, patience, forbearance, forgiveness — and it is held together by love. Verse 16 sets the word of Christ dwelling richly alongside teaching and singing.

4.t: Instruction on speaking to outsiders: wise, gracious, and able to answer each person. Apologetics in one verse, with the manner specified before the content.

1.ctx: Paul writes from prison to a church founded by his co-worker Epaphras. See History & setting of Colossians above.
1.mean: ‘Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace and peace to you from God our Father.’
1.big: Though Paul had never met them, he writes as one family in Christ.

src.l: ‘Colossians, Letter to the’ and ‘Colossians, Letter to the, Critical Issues’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

1.ctx: Epaphras had brought Paul news of the church (1:7–8).
1.mean: Paul thanks God for their ‘faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints—the faith and love proceeding from the hope stored up for you in heaven’. The gospel is ‘bearing fruit and growing’ all over the world, as among them. He prays that God will ‘fill you with the knowledge of His will’, so that they ‘may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord’, with endurance, patience and joyful thanks to the Father, ‘who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.’
1.big: God has rescued believers from darkness into his Son’s kingdom, and Paul prays they will live worthy of it.
1.diff: Notice that the ‘knowledge’ Paul prays for is practical: knowing God’s will so as to live it. The false teachers offered special knowledge; Paul says real knowledge leads to fruit and thanksgiving.

1.ctx: Many think verses 15–20 were an early hymn or confession. They set out who Christ is in relation to creation (15–17) and to the new creation, the church (18–20).
1.mean: ‘The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.’ He is also ‘the head of the body, the church; He is the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence. For God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him, and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things… by making peace through the blood of His cross.’ The Colossians, once ‘alienated from God’, are now reconciled, ‘if indeed you continue in your faith’.
1.big: Christ is the Creator and Sustainer of everything, and the one through whose cross God reconciles all things.
1.diff: ‘Firstborn over all creation’. Jehovah’s Witnesses, following the ancient Arians, take ‘firstborn’ to mean Jesus was the first being God created. Their New World Translation adds the word ‘other’ in verses 16–17: ‘all other things were created’, ‘he is before all other things’. The word ‘other’ is not in the Greek. The historic Christian reading is that ‘firstborn’ means first in rank and the heir, as in Psalm 89:27, where God says of David’s line, ‘I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth’ (David was the youngest son). The next verse explains why he is ‘firstborn’: ‘For in Him all things were created’. He is the Creator, not part of creation. Calvin rejected the Arian argument that the title makes Christ a creature; Wesley glossed ‘firstborn’ as ‘begotten before every creature; subsisting before all worlds, before all time, from all eternity.’ The Nicene Creed confesses the Son as ‘begotten, not made’. ‘Reconcile… all things’ (verse 20) does not mean everyone will be saved; verses 21–23 at once say the Colossians are reconciled ‘if indeed you continue in your faith’. It means Christ’s cross will put the whole universe right.

1.ctx: Paul writes from prison, suffering because of his mission to the Gentiles.
1.mean: ‘Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church.’ His task is to proclaim ‘the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed’: that God’s plan includes the Gentiles, ‘Christ in you, the hope of glory.’ ‘We proclaim Him, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ.’
1.big: Paul gladly suffers so that Christ, ‘the hope of glory’, may be made known to all.
1.diff: ‘What is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions’. This does not mean Christ’s death was not enough to save; Paul has just said peace was made ‘through the blood of His cross’. Most interpreters understand it as the sufferings Christ’s people must still go through in this age, which Christ counts as his own because they are his body (compare Acts 9:4, ‘why do you persecute Me?’). Wesley: ‘That which remains to be suffered by his members.’ Calvin: ‘As, therefore, Christ has suffered once in his own person, so he suffers daily in his members.’ Calvin strongly rejected the medieval use of this verse to support indulgences, the idea that the saints’ extra merits could be applied to others. Catholic teaching today uses the verse to speak of believers uniting their sufferings to Christ’s for the good of the church; the Catechism quotes it in its teaching on the sick (1508).

2.h: Absent in Body, Present in Spirit
2.ctx: Paul has not met the Colossians or the Laodiceans, but he is ‘struggling’ for them in prayer.
2.mean: Paul wants them ‘encouraged in heart, knit together in love’, and to know ‘the mystery of God, namely Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.’ ‘I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric.’ Though absent in body, he delights in their ‘orderly condition and firm faith in Christ.’
2.big: Every treasure of wisdom is found in Christ, so believers need not look anywhere else.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Colossians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

2.ctx: The heart of the letter: Paul answers the false teaching directly. See The ‘Colossian philosophy’ above.
2.mean: ‘Just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him’. ‘See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception’. Why look elsewhere? ‘For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form. And you have been made complete in Christ’. They have had the true circumcision, ‘performed by Christ and not by human hands’, and ‘having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith’. God ‘forgave us all our trespasses, having canceled the debt ascribed to us… nailing it to the cross!’, and disarmed the hostile powers, ‘triumphing over them by the cross.’ ‘Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.’ Rules like ‘Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!’ ‘have an appearance of wisdom’ but ‘are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.’
2.big: Believers are complete in Christ, so rules, rituals and experiences add nothing to him.
2.diff: ‘All the fullness of the Deity… in bodily form’ (verse 9). One of the clearest statements in the New Testament that Christ is fully God and truly human. Wesley: ‘The very substance of God, if one might so speak, dwells in Christ in the most full sense.’ Circumcision and baptism (verses 11–12). Reformed and other churches that baptise infants see here a link between circumcision and baptism as signs of God’s covenant: as Israelite boys were circumcised, so ‘the infants of one, or both, believing parents, are to be baptized’ (Westminster Confession 28.4). Baptists note that verse 12 ties baptism to being raised ‘through your faith’, and hold that only those who ‘actually profess repentance towards God’ and faith should be baptised (1689 Confession 29.2). Calvin, here, simply calls baptism ‘a sign of the thing that is presented to us’. The Sabbath (verse 16). Most Christians read this as showing that the Jewish calendar, including the weekly Sabbath, was a ‘shadow’ fulfilled in Christ, so believers must not be judged for not keeping it. They differ on what follows. Reformed Christians (Westminster Confession 21.7) hold that the Sabbath principle continues, ‘changed into the first day of the week’, ‘the Christian Sabbath’. Calvin was looser: ‘we do not by any means observe days, as though there were any sacredness in holidays.’ Seventh-day Adventists hold that the fourth commandment ‘requires the observance of this seventh-day Sabbath’, and usually read verse 16 as referring only to the special ceremonial sabbaths of Israel’s feasts, not the weekly one. Wesley, however, explicitly included ‘the weekly Jewish sabbaths’. ‘The worship of angels’ (verse 18) may mean worshipping angels, or claiming to join in the angels’ worship in visions. Either way, nothing must be put between believers and Christ.

3.ctx: Paul turns from what believers do not need (the false teachers’ rules) to what really changes a life: being united with Christ.
3.mean: ‘Since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above’. ‘For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God.’ So: ‘Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed, which is idolatry.’ Put aside ‘anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language’. ‘Do not lie to one another’. They have ‘put on the new self’, in which ‘there is no Greek or Jew… slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all.’ ‘Clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience.’ ‘Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love’. ‘Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you’. ‘And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus’.
3.big: Because believers are raised with Christ, they put off the old life and put on Christ’s character, above all love.
3.diff: ‘Greed, which is idolatry’. Paul treats wanting more as worshipping something other than God. It is the sin in this list that respectable churches most often overlook. ‘Scythian’ was a byword for the wildest barbarian. Even such divisions disappear in Christ.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Colossians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

3.ctx: Greek and Roman writers set out duties for households, addressed to the head of the house. Paul addresses wives, children and slaves directly, as responsible believers, and gives the stronger party duties too.
3.mean: ‘Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them. Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged.’
3.big: Christian homes are shaped by love, respect and gentleness, ‘in the Lord’.
3.diff: Submission in marriage. As at Ephesians 5:21–33, Christians differ on how this applies today. Complementarians hold that the husband has a God-given role of loving leadership and the wife of willing support, which reflects Christ and the church. Egalitarians hold that these instructions applied the gospel within the household customs of the time, and that the principle is mutual submission and love. Both are held by evangelicals who take Scripture seriously. All agree that ‘submit’ never means accepting abuse, and that husbands are commanded to love and not be harsh. A church’s leaders can help where a marriage is struggling or unsafe.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Colossians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

3.ctx: Slaves made up a large part of the population of Roman cities and of the early church. Onesimus, a runaway slave from Colossae, carried this letter home (4:9).
3.mean: ‘Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, not only to please them while they are watching, but with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord. Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for men’. ‘It is the Lord Christ you are serving.’ ‘Whoever does wrong will be repaid for his wrong, and there is no favoritism.’
3.big: Ordinary work, even the lowest, is done for Christ and will be rewarded by him.
3.diff: Paul is not endorsing slavery. He is telling believers who had no choice how to live faithfully in it, and he addresses masters too (4:1). In his letter to Philemon he asks a master to receive his slave back ‘as a beloved brother’ (Philemon 16). Christians today apply these verses to employees and employers, while recognising that paid work is very different from slavery.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Colossians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: Paul finishes the household instructions and then turns to prayer and witness.
4.mean: ‘Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven.’ ‘Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful’, and pray for Paul, that God ‘may open to us a door for the word’. ‘Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.’
4.big: Prayer and gracious speech go together in a church that wants outsiders to hear the gospel.
4.diff: Verse 1’s reminder that masters have ‘a Master in heaven’ is one of the principles later Christians drew on in opposing slavery.

src.l: Calvin, Commentary on Colossians (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: The same people send greetings at the end of Philemon (verses 23–24), which ties the two letters together.
4.mean: Tychicus is bringing the letter, with ‘Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.’ Greetings come from Aristarchus, ‘Mark the cousin of Barnabas’, and Jesus Justus: ‘These are the only Jews among my fellow workers’. Then Epaphras, ‘always wrestling in prayer for you’, and ‘Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas’.
4.big: The gospel created a team of very different people, and even a runaway slave became ‘our faithful and beloved brother’.
4.diff: Mark is almost certainly John Mark, who had deserted Paul on his first journey and caused a sharp split between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39). Now Paul commends him. Tradition names him as the author of Mark’s Gospel. Luke. Since Paul lists Aristarchus, Mark and Justus as ‘the only Jews’ with him, Luke, named separately, was probably a Gentile, making him the only non-Jewish writer of New Testament books (Luke and Acts). Demas later deserted Paul, ‘in his love of this world’ (2 Timothy 4:10).

4.ctx: Early churches met in homes. Paul’s letters were read aloud to the gathered church and passed between congregations.
4.mean: ‘Greet the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha and the church that meets at her house.’ ‘After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.’ A word for Archippus: ‘See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord.’ Then Paul’s own hand: ‘Remember my chains. Grace be with you.’
4.big: Paul’s letters were meant to be shared between churches, a first step towards the New Testament.
4.diff: The letter from Laodicea was probably a letter Paul had sent to Laodicea, to be passed on. Most scholars think it was lost early. Some suggest it is our Ephesians, perhaps a circular letter; the 2nd-century teacher Marcion believed Ephesians had been addressed to Laodicea. A short ‘Letter to the Laodiceans’ found in some early Latin Bibles claims to be it, but it is a patchwork of phrases from Paul’s other letters, written between the 2nd and 4th centuries, and the Second Council of Nicaea (AD 787) denounced it as a forgery.
